scenario: A platform team at Contoso is setting up a new generative AI initiative in Microsoft Foundry and needs to decide how to structure the workspace before onboarding multiple product teams.
question: Which structure does Microsoft recommend for new agent and model work, giving each team an isolated workspace under shared governance?
options: Hub-based projects under a shared Foundry hub
A standalone Azure OpenAI resource per team
A separate Azure Machine Learning workspace per team
Foundry projects under a single Foundry resource
explanation: D is correct: the Foundry resource is the top-level governance boundary (networking, security, model deployments, connections) and each Foundry project is an isolated development boundary inside it, so several teams can reuse shared deployments and connections without repeated IT setup. New agent capabilities, including the generally available Foundry Agent Service, are only available on Foundry projects. A is wrong because hub-based projects appear only in the Foundry (classic) portal and are now kept for classic-only features such as prompt flow or managed compute deployments. C is wrong because an Azure Machine Learning workspace lacks the Foundry project experience for agents, evaluations and the model catalog. B is wrong because a standalone Azure OpenAI resource only serves model calls, without agent hosting or evaluations, and Microsoft provides an upgrade path from it to a Foundry resource.

scenario: A developer wants to evaluate several LLMs — an Azure OpenAI model, a Meta Llama model, and a Cohere model — before committing to one for a new chatbot.
question: Where in Microsoft Foundry can the developer browse and compare these models from multiple providers side by side?
explanation: The model catalog is the central hub for browsing first-party (Azure OpenAI, Phi), partner, and open-source models (Meta Llama, Mistral, Cohere, DeepSeek, and more), including benchmarks, licensing, and supported deployment options for each. Azure AI Search is a retrieval/indexing service, Content Safety Studio is for moderation configuration, and Azure Monitor is for observability — none browse or compare models.

scenario: A team wants to deploy a partner model from the model catalog, whose model card lists serverless deployment, without provisioning or managing any virtual machines, paying only for the tokens they consume.
question: Which deployment option should they choose?
options: Managed compute (real-time endpoint on a dedicated VM)
explanation: D is correct: a serverless (pay-per-token) deployment exposes the model through an API that Microsoft hosts and manages, billed per input and output token, with no virtual machines in your subscription. A is wrong because managed compute deploys the model weights to dedicated VMs that are billed for core hours whether or not traffic arrives. C is wrong because a local ONNX export moves hosting onto infrastructure the team would have to run themselves. B is wrong because provisioned throughput reserves capacity that is billed hourly, which is the opposite of paying only for the tokens consumed.

scenario: A financial-services customer needs an Azure OpenAI chat model deployment with guaranteed, consistent low latency for a real-time trading assistant and is willing to commit to reserved capacity.
question: Which Azure OpenAI deployment type best fits this requirement?
explanation: Provisioned throughput (PTU) reserves dedicated model capacity for a customer, delivering predictable, consistent latency and throughput — ideal for latency-sensitive production workloads willing to commit to reserved units. Standard and Global Standard are shared, pay-as-you-go capacity with variable latency under load. Global Batch is for large, non-latency-sensitive asynchronous jobs processed within a 24-hour window at a discount.

scenario: A developer is building a RAG chatbot in Microsoft Foundry and needs the project to retrieve passages from a private knowledge base at query time.
question: What must the developer add to the Foundry project to enable this retrieval-augmented generation pattern?
options: A connection to an Azure AI Search resource with a populated vector/hybrid index
A second Azure OpenAI deployment for redundancy
explanation: RAG requires an external index the model can query for grounding context — in Microsoft Foundry this is typically an Azure AI Search connection with a vector or hybrid index built over the private documents. Extra model deployments don't provide retrieval; Content Safety and Prompt Shields address moderation and injection defense, not grounding.

scenario: A developer writing Python automation needs to list a Foundry project's connections and read its project properties during environment setup, separate from making inference calls to a deployed model.
question: Which SDK is purpose-built for these project-level setup tasks, as distinct from the SDK used for chat and embedding calls?
explanation: C is correct: azure-ai-projects (2.x targets the current Foundry portal) provides the project client, which handles Foundry-native operations such as listing connections, retrieving project properties and enabling tracing, and can also give you an OpenAI-compatible client for model calls. A is wrong because azure-ai-inference was retired on August 26, 2026, and Microsoft's migration path for inference is the openai package. B is wrong because the openai package makes the chat completions, embeddings and Responses API calls themselves, not project setup calls. D is wrong because azure-storage-blob manages blob storage, not Foundry projects.

scenario: A team wants to fine-tune a base model on their own labeled support-ticket conversations to improve response tone and format.
question: What format must the training data file use when submitting a fine-tuning job in Microsoft Foundry?
options: A CSV file with two columns: prompt and completion
A JSONL file where each line is a conversation object with a messages array of role/content pairs
A plain .txt file with one example per paragraph
A Parquet file exported from Azure AI Search
explanation: Fine-tuning jobs expect a JSONL file, one JSON object per line, each containing a messages array (system/user/assistant turns) matching the chat-completion message format — mirroring how the model will be used in production. CSV, plain text, and Parquet are not accepted training-data formats for this pipeline.

scenario: An architect is estimating throughput limits before load-testing a new Azure OpenAI deployment.
question: Which two quota dimensions does Azure OpenAI enforce per deployment to control capacity consumption?
options: Number of connections and number of projects
explanation: Azure OpenAI quota is expressed and enforced in tokens-per-minute (TPM) and requests-per-minute (RPM) per deployment, and these can be adjusted (within subscription limits) or split across multiple deployments. The other options are infrastructure metrics that aren't how Azure OpenAI quota is modeled.

scenario: A prompt engineer wants to quickly iterate on a system message and a couple of few-shot examples before writing any application code.
question: Which Microsoft Foundry feature is designed for this rapid, code-free iteration?
explanation: The chat playground lets you adjust the system message, parameters (temperature, top-p), and try few-shot examples interactively, then view the equivalent code/JSON to carry into your app — no code required for the iteration itself. The other options are for evaluation, building agents programmatically, and observability, respectively — later stages of the workflow.

scenario: A platform team must onboard three product teams that need the same network and security posture, the same shared model deployments, and separate workspaces for their own agents and files.
question: What is the main architectural benefit of putting all three teams' projects under one Foundry resource?
options: It removes the need for any network security configuration
It exempts the projects from guardrail and content filtering requirements
It automatically merges all teams' data into one fine-tuned model
It centralizes governance, deployments and connections that each project can reuse
explanation: D is correct: the Foundry resource is where networking, security settings, model deployments and shared connections are managed, while each project is a development boundary with its own agents, files and evaluations. Teams reuse those shared settings without each one re-creating them. A is wrong because the resource is where network isolation is configured, so the work still has to be done once. C is wrong because projects keep their data isolated, and nothing merges it into a fine-tuned model. B is wrong because guardrails apply to model deployments and agents regardless of how projects are grouped.

scenario: Before committing to a model for a cost-sensitive, high-volume summarization feature, a team wants to compare quality, latency, and cost trade-offs across several catalog models.
question: Which model catalog feature directly supports this comparison?
explanation: Model benchmarks in the catalog show comparative quality, cost, and throughput/latency metrics across models on standard datasets, helping teams shortlist candidates before deployment. The other listed features relate to safety configuration and agent conversation state, not model comparison.

scenario: A compliance reviewer asks whether a team deploying an Azure OpenAI chat model in Microsoft Foundry can switch off all output content filtering for an internal red-teaming exercise.
question: What is true about default guardrails on Foundry Models sold by Azure?
options: Guardrails are optional add-ons that stay off until a project owner enables them
Guardrails only apply to image-generation models, not to text models
Any project owner can turn off input and output filtering at any time
A default guardrail applies; turning off output filtering needs approval for modified guardrails
explanation: D is correct: model deployments get the Microsoft.DefaultV2 guardrail by default. Every customer can choose Low, Medium or High blocking levels and can turn content-harm filtering off for inputs, but only customers approved through the Limited Access Review for modified guardrails can turn it off for outputs. A is wrong because filtering is on from the start, not opt-in. C is wrong because turning off output filtering is not self-service. B is wrong because the guardrail system applies to text models as well as image models; only audio transcription models are excluded.

scenario: A team maintains a Prompt flow that chains a retrieval step, a prompt template and an LLM call, and serves it from a managed online endpoint. They are planning next year's roadmap.
question: What does Microsoft recommend for this workload?
options: Rebuild it as a Connected Agents tool in the new Foundry Agent Service
Keep extending it, because Prompt flow is the main low-code tool in the new portal
Migrate it to Microsoft Agent Framework before Prompt flow retires on April 20, 2027
Package it as a custom model and publish it to the model catalog
explanation: C is correct: Prompt flow is no longer recommended for new development and retires on April 20, 2027. Its runtime container images no longer receive security or package updates, and Microsoft's migration guide maps flows to Agent Framework's WorkflowBuilder, executors and edges. B is wrong because Prompt flow is a classic-only feature that the new Foundry portal doesn't offer, so extending it adds to the migration debt. A is wrong because the Connected Agents tool is not available in the new Foundry Agent Service. D is wrong because the model catalog lists models, not orchestration code, so publishing there does nothing to replace the flow.

scenario: A team based in a region where a newly released frontier model isn't yet listed as deployable discovers their deployment attempt fails.
question: What is the most likely explanation?
options: Microsoft Foundry requires a support ticket for every deployment
All models are globally available immediately upon catalog release
Model availability in the catalog is region-specific, and the model may not yet be offered in that region/deployment type
explanation: Catalog models — especially newly released ones — roll out to specific Azure regions and specific deployment types (serverless API vs. managed compute vs. Azure OpenAI SKUs) incrementally, not globally and instantly. Checking the model card's region/deployment availability is the standard troubleshooting step, not filing a ticket or assuming subscription issues.

scenario: An architect explaining Microsoft Foundry to a new hire summarizes the platform's core value proposition.
question: Which statement best captures what Microsoft Foundry unifies into a single platform?
options: Only image-generation models and their licensing terms
Exclusively Azure Machine Learning's classic ML pipeline designer
Agents, models and tools, with tracing, evaluation and governance under one resource
A replacement for Microsoft Entra ID identity management
explanation: C is correct: Microsoft Foundry (formerly Azure AI Foundry) brings agents, models and tools together under one Azure resource, with tracing, monitoring, evaluations, role-based access control, networking and policies managed in one place. A is wrong because the catalog covers chat, reasoning, embedding and multimodal models, not only image generation. B is wrong because Foundry targets generative AI apps and agents, not the classic ML pipeline designer. D is wrong because Foundry uses Microsoft Entra ID for identity; it doesn't replace it.

scenario: A developer finds Microsoft Learn pages for Speech, Vision, Language and Content Safety grouped under the name 'Foundry Tools' and wonders whether this is a new product line.
question: What were the Foundry Tools previously called?
explanation: D is correct: Microsoft renamed its AI services portfolio from Azure Cognitive Services to Azure AI Services and then to Foundry Tools, alongside the platform's own rename from Azure AI Studio to Azure AI Foundry to Microsoft Foundry. The Azure resource type is still Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts. B is wrong because Azure Machine Learning is a separate ML platform that still uses its own name. C is wrong because Azure AI Search keeps its name and appears in Foundry as a connected resource. A is wrong because Logic Apps is a workflow-integration service outside the AI portfolio.

scenario: An EU insurer needs pay-per-token billing for an Azure OpenAI chat model with unpredictable traffic, and its policy requires that prompts and completions are processed only within the EU.
question: Which deployment type best fits both requirements?
explanation: C is correct: Data Zone Standard is billed per token and keeps inference processing within the data-zone boundary, so EU deployments stay in the EU. A is wrong because global deployments might route processing to any Azure region, which breaks the residency rule. B is wrong because provisioned deployments bill hourly for reserved capacity, a poor fit for unpredictable traffic. D is wrong because batch is asynchronous, with results returned later, and global batch also processes across regions.
